title: Robin Hood
author: Howard Pyle
ru: Английская легенда о благородном разбойнике Робин Гуде и его весёлых друзьях из Шервудского леса.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. Robin Becomes an Outlaw
chapters.text:
Long ago, in the middle of England, there was a great forest called Sherwood. It was full of old oak trees, and the king's deer lived there. Nobody could hunt them. Only the king could.

Near the forest lived a young man called Robin Hood. He was eighteen, tall and strong, with a quick smile. And he could shoot with a bow better than anyone in the country.

One spring morning Robin took his bow and set off for the town of Nottingham. There was a shooting match there, and the prize was a barrel of beer. Robin whistled as he walked.

Under an oak tree sat fifteen foresters — the king's men, who looked after the forest. They were eating and drinking.

“Hey, boy!” one of them called. “Where are you going with that little bow? Go home to your mother!”

Robin's face went red. “I'll bet you twenty pounds,” he said, “that I can hit a deer from two hundred metres.”

“Go on, then!” they laughed, and they pointed at some deer far away across the field.

Robin pulled the string back to his ear. Twang! The arrow flew across the field, and the biggest deer fell down dead.

“Twenty pounds, please,” said Robin.

But the foresters were angry now. “That was the king's deer!” shouted the oldest one. “Get out of here, quickly!”

Robin turned and walked away. Then — whizz! An arrow flew past his head, so close that he felt the wind. The old forester was shooting at him!

Robin didn't stop to think. He turned and shot back. The forester fell to the ground and did not get up again.

Robin ran deep into the forest. “What have I done?” he cried. “I only wanted to go to a shooting match. And now a man is dead because of me.”

He could never go home now. He was an outlaw — a man outside the law. The Sheriff of Nottingham, the most powerful man in the town, said: “Two hundred pounds to the man who brings me Robin Hood, dead or alive!”

So Robin stayed in Sherwood, but he was not alone for long. Other men came to the forest: poor men, hungry men, men with no home. Some killed the king's deer because their children were hungry. Some lost their land to rich lords.

“From today,” Robin told them, “we take from the rich, and we give to the poor. And we never hurt a woman, a child or a poor man.”

The men dressed in green, so nobody could see them among the leaves. They laughed and sang all day, and people called them the Merry Men.

A year went by. Then one morning Robin stood up and stretched. “Life is too quiet,” he said. “I'm going to look for an adventure. Stay here, but listen for my horn.”

And off he went, alone, into the forest.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. Little John on the Bridge
chapters.text:
Robin walked until he came to a wide river. The bridge over it was just a fallen tree, so narrow that only one man could cross at a time.

Robin stepped onto the bridge. At the same moment a stranger stepped onto the other end. He was a giant of a man, a head taller than Robin, with shoulders as wide as a door. In his hand he had a long, thick stick — a staff.

“Go back,” Robin called, “and let the better man cross first.”

“Then stay where you are,” said the stranger, “because I am the better man.”

Robin took an arrow out. “Go back, or I'll send this arrow through you.”

The giant laughed. “You have a bow, and I have only a stick. What a brave man!”

Robin's face went hot. He put down his bow and cut a staff for himself from an oak tree.

“Now it's fair,” he said. “The man who falls in the water loses.”

They met in the middle. Crack! Bang! Crack! The birds flew up out of the trees. Robin was fast. He hit the giant on the head, and a little blood ran down his face. But the giant didn't fall. He only got angry. He lifted his great staff and — bang! — he hit Robin so hard that Robin flew off the bridge.

Splash!

“Ha!” the giant shouted, looking down. “Where are you now, my good man?”

Robin's head came up out of the water. “Going down the river,” he answered. Then he began to laugh. He climbed out onto the grass, all wet.

“You're a strong man and a good fighter,” he said. “I lost, and I'm happy to say it.”

He put his horn to his lips and blew. Soon twenty men in green came running through the trees, with Robin's friend Will Stutely in front.

“Robin! Why are you so wet?”

“This man threw me into the river,” said Robin.

“Then let's throw him in too!” shouted the Merry Men.

“No, stop!” said Robin. “He won fairly.” He turned to the stranger. “Come and live with us in Sherwood, my friend. You can have a bow, a green coat and as much food as you want.”

The giant smiled and held out his big hand. “Then I'm with you.”

“What's your name?” asked Robin.

“John Little.”

Will Stutely laughed loudly. “John Little? Look at him — he's as big as a house! No, no. From today, his name is Little John!”

Everyone laughed, and the giant laughed loudest of all.

That night there was a great feast under the trees. From that day Little John was always by Robin's side.

But in Nottingham, someone was not laughing. The Sheriff sat in his big house, red in the face.

“Robin Hood is laughing at me,” he said. “But I'll catch him. You'll see.”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Robin the Butcher
chapters.text:
The Sheriff sent his soldiers into Sherwood again and again. But the forest was big and dark, and the Merry Men knew every tree. The soldiers always came home tired, hungry and without Robin.

One day, on the road near the forest, Robin met a butcher. He had a horse and a cart full of meat, and he was going to the market in Nottingham.

“How much for everything?” asked Robin. “The horse, the cart, the meat and your coat?”

The butcher laughed. “Oh, five pounds, I think.”

Robin gave him six. So the butcher walked home with a big smile, and Robin, in the butcher's coat, drove the cart into Nottingham.

At the market he shouted, “Meat! Good meat! Very cheap!”

And it was very cheap. The other butchers sold a piece of meat for five pennies. Robin sold it for one. Soon every woman in town was at his table, and the other butchers had nothing to do.

“Who is this fool?” they asked each other. “Maybe he's the son of a rich man, and he's throwing away his father's money.”

The Sheriff heard about the strange young butcher, and his small eyes shone. A rich young fool? That was good news. He invited Robin to dinner.

At the dinner Robin ate a lot, laughed a lot and paid for everyone's wine.

“Tell me,” said the Sheriff, “do you have any animals to sell? Cows, maybe?”

“Oh, yes!” said Robin. “I have five hundred horned animals. They're near here, but I don't know what to do with them. You can have them all for three hundred pounds.”

Five hundred animals for three hundred pounds! The Sheriff almost jumped out of his chair.

The next morning he took a bag with three hundred pounds in gold and rode out with Robin. They left the road and went into the trees, deeper and deeper.

The Sheriff began to look around nervously. “I don't like this forest,” he said. “Robin Hood lives here.”

“Don't worry,” said Robin. “I know Robin Hood well. He isn't going to hurt you today.”

Just then they came to an open place. A hundred deer were eating the grass there.

“There!” said Robin. “Those are my horned animals. Aren't they beautiful?”

The Sheriff's face went white. Robin put his horn to his lips and blew, and the Merry Men came out of the trees from every side.

“Welcome to Sherwood, Sheriff!” said Little John. “You're just in time for dinner.”

It was a very good dinner. The Sheriff didn't enjoy it at all.

After dinner Robin took the Sheriff's bag of gold. “You must pay for your meal, my friend,” he said. “And the meat was very good, so the price is three hundred pounds.”

Then he put the Sheriff on his horse and sent him home.

“I'll catch you, Robin Hood!” the Sheriff shouted over his shoulder.

The Merry Men laughed until they cried.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Friar Tuck
chapters.text:
One summer evening the Merry Men were shooting at a target, and Robin hit the centre every time.

“There's no better man with a bow in England,” said Little John.

But Will Scarlet, a young man who always wore red, shook his head. “I know a man who is better,” he said. “He lives by the river, near Fountains Abbey. He's a friar — a man of the church, like a monk. He can shoot, he can fight with a sword, and nobody can beat him.”

“Then I'm going to meet this friar,” said Robin.

The next day he came to the river. Under a tree sat a fat man in a long brown robe, with a round red face. He had a big meat pie in one hand and a bottle in the other, and he was singing to himself.

Robin pointed an arrow at him. “Good afternoon, friar. Carry me across the river on your back. I don't want to get my feet wet.”

The friar put down his pie and looked at the arrow. Then, without a word, he lifted Robin onto his back and walked across the river.

On the other side Robin jumped down. But now the friar had a sword in his hand, and its point was at Robin's chest.

“Now, my fine young man,” said the friar sweetly, “carry me back. I don't want to get my feet wet either.”

So Robin carried him back. The friar was very, very heavy, and Robin's legs were shaking by the end.

Then Robin pulled out his own sword. “And now,” he said, “carry me across again.”

“Of course,” said the friar. He lifted Robin up and walked out into the river. In the middle, where the water was deep, he stopped.

“Sink or swim, my friend!” he said, and he threw Robin into the river.

Splash!

Robin came up, angry and wet, and the fight began. They fought for an hour, then another hour, and neither man could win.

At last Robin stepped back. “Let me blow my horn three times,” he said.

“Blow until your eyes fall out,” said the friar.

Robin blew. Soon fifty men in green came running.

“Ah,” said the friar. “Then let me whistle three times.”

He whistled, and fifty big dogs came running out of the trees, barking and showing their teeth.

But then Will Scarlet ran forward. “Stop! Stop, Tuck!” he shouted. “It's me, Will! This man is Robin Hood!”

The friar's mouth fell open. “Robin Hood? Why didn't you say so? I threw Robin Hood into the river!” And he laughed so hard that his big stomach shook.

“Come and live with us,” said Robin, laughing too. “We need a man of the church who can fight like you.”

So Friar Tuck came to Sherwood with his sword and his songs, and he never left. And very soon, Robin had a job for him.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. A Wedding in the Forest
chapters.text:
One morning a young man walked past Robin's hiding place by the road. He had a harp on his back, and he was singing like a bird. The next morning the same young man came past again. But now his head was down, and his face was grey and sad.

Robin stepped out of the trees. “What's wrong, my friend? Yesterday you were singing.”

“My name is Allan a Dale,” said the young man. “Yesterday I was happy, because I was going to marry Ellen, the most beautiful girl in the world. We love each other. But now her father says no. He is going to give her to Sir Stephen, a rich knight — so old that he walks with a stick and has almost no teeth. The wedding is tomorrow.”

Robin thought for a moment, then smiled.

“Allan,” he said, “tomorrow there is going to be a wedding. But maybe it won't be Sir Stephen's.”

The next day the little church near Sherwood was full of flowers. At the front stood the Bishop of Hereford, an important man of the church — fat, rich and dressed in gold.

An old man with a harp and a long grey beard came into the church. It was Robin.

“Who are you?” asked the Bishop.

“I play music at weddings,” said Robin. “But I can only play when the two young people love each other.”

Then Sir Stephen arrived, slowly, on his stick. Behind him came Ellen with her father. She was very pretty, but pale, with tears in her eyes.

“This is not a good wedding,” said Robin loudly. “Look at the girl. She doesn't love this old man.”

“Be quiet, you old fool!” said the Bishop.

But Robin put his horn to his lips and blew. The church doors opened, and in came Little John, Will Scarlet, Friar Tuck — and Allan a Dale. Ellen gave a cry and ran to him.

Sir Stephen looked at all the bows and swords. “Keep the girl,” he said. “I don't want a wife from the forest!” And he hurried out of the church as fast as his old legs could go.

“Now, Bishop,” said Robin, “marry Allan and Ellen.”

“No!” said the Bishop, and he folded his arms.

“Then I'll do it,” said Friar Tuck happily.

Ellen's father was angry, but Robin opened a bag. “Here are two hundred pounds,” he said. “For the bride's father, with love from Robin Hood.”

The father looked at the gold, and suddenly he was much less angry.

So Friar Tuck married Allan and Ellen, and Ellen smiled for the first time that day. Then everyone went back to Sherwood for a wedding feast — the Bishop too, because Robin wanted him there.

“And who is going to pay for the feast?” asked Little John.

Robin looked at the fat Bishop and his heavy gold rings, and he smiled.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Sad Knight
chapters.text:
“Little John,” said Robin one day, “I don't want to eat alone today. Go to the road and find me a guest — a rich one.”

Little John and Will Scarlet waited by the road. At last a knight came along on a tired horse. His clothes were old, and he had the saddest face in all England.

“Good sir,” said Little John, “our master invites you to dinner.” The knight didn't even ask who their master was. He only sighed and followed them.

Under the great oak tree there was a fine dinner of deer meat, bread and wine. The knight ate quietly, and slowly his face got a little less sad.

“Thank you,” he said at last.

“You're welcome,” said Robin. “But here in Sherwood the guests pay for their dinner. How much money do you have?”

“Only ten shillings,” said the knight. “I'm sorry. It's all I have.”

Little John opened the knight's bag and looked inside. “It's true, Robin. Ten shillings — and nothing more.”

“How can a knight be so poor?” asked Robin, surprised.

The knight looked down. “My name is Sir Richard of the Lea. My son got into a fight and killed a man. To save him from prison, I borrowed four hundred pounds from the Abbot of St Mary's.”

“An abbot?” said Friar Tuck. “The head of a big, rich abbey?”

“Yes. And in three days I must give the money back. I don't have it, so the Abbot is going to take my castle and all my land. He's very happy about it.”

The Merry Men were silent. Then Robin stood up.

“Little John,” he said, “bring four hundred pounds from our money.”

Sir Richard looked up. “What?”

“It's not a gift,” said Robin. “It's a loan. You can pay us back in a year.”

The Merry Men didn't stop there. Little John brought cloth for new clothes. He measured it with his long bow, and every time he added an extra metre. Will Scarlet brought a fine horse, and Friar Tuck brought new boots.

Sir Richard had tears in his eyes. “I'll never forget this,” he said.

Three days later, Sir Richard walked into St Mary's Abbey in his old clothes. He wanted to see the Abbot's face. The fat Abbot was at dinner with his rich friends.

“Ah, Sir Richard,” said the Abbot with a smile. “Do you have my money? No? Then your castle is mine!”

“Wait,” said the knight. He opened a heavy bag, and gold poured out onto the table.

“Four hundred pounds,” said Sir Richard. “Every penny.”

The Abbot's smile disappeared. His face went red, then white, then green. And Sir Richard walked out into the sunshine, laughing.

A year later he came back to Sherwood with the money and a present: a hundred fine bows.

But that same week, the Sheriff of Nottingham had a new idea.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. The Golden Arrow
chapters.text:
Soon there was news all over the country: a great shooting match in Nottingham! The prize was an arrow made of gold.

“Robin Hood loves shooting,” the Sheriff said to himself with a smile. “He can't stay away from a match like this. And when he comes, my soldiers are going to be ready.”

In Sherwood, Little John shook his head. “It's a trap,” he said. “Don't go, Robin.”

“A golden arrow!” said Robin. “All the best archers in England are going to be there. I'm not staying at home.” He smiled. “But I'm not going as Robin Hood.”

On the day of the match Robin dressed in old red clothes full of holes. He put a patch over one eye and dirt on his face. Now he looked like a poor old beggar. The Merry Men went too, one by one, dressed as farmers, beggars and monks.

The field outside Nottingham was full of people. The Sheriff sat in a big chair, with soldiers all around him, and looked at every face in the crowd.

“Where are the men in green?” he whispered to his captain. “Is Robin Hood here?”

“No, sir. There's nobody in green today.”

The match began. One by one, the worst archers went home, until only three were left: Gilbert of the White Hand, a famous archer; Adam of the Dell; and the old beggar in red.

Gilbert shot. His arrow hit the target near the centre. The people cheered.

Adam shot. His arrow hit even closer. The people cheered more loudly.

Then the beggar stepped forward. He pulled back the string — slowly, carefully — and let the arrow go. It hit the target right in the centre.

For a moment the field was silent. Then everyone threw their hats in the air.

The Sheriff gave the golden arrow to the beggar. “Here, my man. You shoot better than that coward Robin Hood. He was too afraid to come today! Come and work for me. I'll pay you well.”

“No, thank you,” said the beggar. “I work for nobody.” And he walked away into the crowd.

That night in Sherwood, the golden arrow shone in the firelight, and the Merry Men sang. But Robin was quiet.

“What's wrong?” asked Little John.

“The Sheriff called me a coward,” said Robin. “He thinks I wasn't there. I want him to know the truth.”

Little John smiled. “Leave it to me.”

The next evening the Sheriff was having dinner in his great hall. Suddenly an arrow flew in through the open window and hit the table, right next to his plate. There was a letter on it.

The Sheriff opened it with shaking hands and read:

“Thank you for the golden arrow. The old beggar in red was Robin Hood.”

The Sheriff jumped up and threw his cup at the wall. This time, he decided, he was going to find a man as dangerous as Robin Hood.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Guy of Gisbourne
chapters.text:
His name was Guy of Gisbourne. He was big and cruel, and he killed people for money. He wore a horse's skin over his clothes, with the horse's head on top of his own, like a hat. People said he could shoot as well as Robin Hood.

“Bring me Robin Hood,” said the Sheriff, “and I'll give you two hundred pounds.”

On the same day, Little John went to Nottingham to buy bread. The Sheriff's soldiers saw him, and ten of them jumped on him at once. They tied him to a tree in the Sheriff's garden.

“Tomorrow you're going to hang,” said the Sheriff happily. “And soon Robin Hood is going to hang next to you.”

Robin knew nothing about this. He was walking alone in Sherwood when he met something very strange: half a man and half a horse. It was Guy of Gisbourne.

“Good morning, stranger,” said Robin. “What are you doing in the forest?”

“I'm looking for an outlaw,” said Guy. “Robin Hood. Do you know where he is?”

“Maybe,” said Robin. “But first, let's have a shooting game. I want to see how good you are.”

They put a small stick in the ground a long way off. Guy shot first. His arrow went near the stick, but missed it. Robin shot next — and split the stick in two.

Guy's eyes went wide. “You shoot like the devil! Who are you?”

“Robin Hood.”

Guy pulled out his sword with a cry, and Robin pulled out his. Guy was strong, and he fought like an angry bull. Then Robin's foot caught on a root, and he fell on his back.

Guy lifted his sword over him. “Now you're going to die, Robin Hood!”

But Robin rolled away just in time. The sword went into the ground. Robin jumped up, and with one quick move he ended the fight. Guy of Gisbourne fell to the ground, and he never got up again.

Just then Will Stutely ran up through the trees. “Robin! The Sheriff has Little John! They're going to hang him tomorrow!”

Robin looked at the horse skin and Guy's silver horn, and he had an idea. He put on the skin and hid his face under the horse's head. Then he walked to Nottingham and blew Guy's horn.

The Sheriff heard the horn and ran out into his garden. “That's Guy's horn! Robin Hood is dead!” he cried. “Guy, my friend, you can have anything you want!”

“I don't want money,” said Robin in a deep voice. “Just let me kill Robin Hood's big friend.”

“Take him!” laughed the Sheriff.

Little John looked up at the horse's head, and his face went white. But then he heard a whisper: “Be ready, John.”

Robin cut the ropes and put a bow and arrows into Little John's hands. Then he threw off the horse skin.

“Robin Hood!” screamed the Sheriff.

Little John pointed an arrow at the Sheriff. The Sheriff turned and ran, and his soldiers ran after him. Robin and Little John walked out of Nottingham, laughing, and nobody tried to stop them.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The King in the Forest
chapters.text:
Years went by. The old king died, and his son Richard was the new king. People called him Richard the Lionheart, because he was as brave as a lion.

King Richard heard many stories about Robin Hood. “Some people call him a thief,” he said. “Others call him a hero. I want to see him with my own eyes.”

So the king put on the robe of a friar and rode into Sherwood with a few of his knights, all dressed as friars too.

Soon a tall man in green stepped out onto the road. “Stop, good friars!” said Robin Hood. “You must have dinner with us.”

Under the great oak tree there was a fine feast. Then Robin said, “Now, let's have a shooting game. Anyone who misses the target gets a punch on the head — from me!”

The Merry Men shot one by one. Some missed, and Robin's punches knocked them over. Then Robin shot — and his arrow just missed.

“Robin missed!” the men shouted happily.

“Then I must take my punch too,” said Robin, and he turned to the tall friar. “You can do it, friar.”

The friar rolled up his sleeve. He hit Robin so hard that Robin fell flat on the grass.

Robin sat up. “What an arm!” he said. “Who are you, friar?”

Just then Sir Richard of the Lea rode up. He looked at the tall friar, jumped off his horse and knelt down in front of him.

“Your Majesty!” he said.

Robin looked again at the friar's face. Then he too fell on his knees, and all his men knelt behind him.

“Forgive us, my king,” said Robin. “We are outlaws, but we love our king.”

King Richard laughed. “I came to find a thief,” he said, “and I found an honest man. I forgive you all. From today you are free men. And Robin, I want you and your men to come to London with me.”

So Robin went to London and served the king. But the city was noisy and grey, and he dreamed of the green trees every night. After some years he came home to Sherwood.

When he was old, Robin got very sick. Little John carried him to a house near the forest, and he lay in bed by the window.

“John,” he said quietly, “give me my bow.”

Little John's hands were shaking as he gave it to him. Robin put an arrow on the string, and with the last of his strength he shot it out of the window, high over the trees.

“Bury me where that arrow falls,” he said. “Bury me under the green trees.”

And there, under an old oak tree in Sherwood, Little John buried his friend.

The Merry Men are gone now. But people say that when the wind moves through the leaves in Sherwood Forest, you can still hear them laughing.
